notes.title: Why these numbers — the physics behind it
notes.p1: With a person standing at midspan the webbing forms a V. Vertical equilibrium at the load point gives sin θ = W / (2T), hence S = (L/2)·tan θ. The webbing's own weight adds a parabola on top, but at 65 g/m it is marginal: over 100 m at 10 kN it contributes 8 cm against the 2 m the person contributes. The real shape of a loaded slackline is always a V with barely curved arms.
notes.h2: Tension is not a fixed input
notes.p2: This is the important difference from the previous version of this calculator. Stepping onto the webbing stretches it, and stretching means more tension. The final tension comes from imposing elastic compatibility between geometry and Hooke's law:
notes.p2b: which is solved numerically (it has a unique root). In the default scenario a 3 kN pre-tension rises to 4.2 kN under the person, and the sag drops from the 4.62 m the constant-tension formula would give to a real 3.38 m. As a side effect the bogus "infinite sag" case disappears — the one that showed up when tension was below W/2. A real line has no infinite sag; it simply stretches until it finds equilibrium.
notes.h3: Why a long line looks almost straight
notes.p3: At fixed tension the angle of the V does not depend on the span: there is no L in sin θ = W/(2T). Sag in metres grows linearly with span — 200 m sags ten times more than 20 m at the same tension. Longer is deeper, not flatter.
notes.p3b: What actually flattens a longline is tension, and longlines are rigged far harder. The absolute sag ends up similar; what changes almost fourfold is the sag-to-span ratio, which is exactly what the eye reads as "V" or "straight":
notes.p3c: That is why the chart is drawn at true 1:1 scale, with the same metres per pixel horizontally and vertically. The effect appears on its own, with no tricks. The vertical exaggeration slider exists only so you can look closely at a very small sag; while it sits at ×1 the drawing does not lie.
notes.p4: Standing, your harness is above the webbing and the leash is slack. When you fall you free-fall your own height above the webbing plus the leash length. Then the leash takes load and brakes: webbing and leash act as two springs in series. The lowest point comes from conservation of energy,
notes.p4b: where z(F) is your depth for a leash force F, and the webbing's sag under that force comes from the same static solver. What dominates the result is not the free fall but how far the webbing stretches: in the default scenario the webbing goes from 3.4 m of sag to 7.1 m, and you end up 12.3 m below the anchors having travelled almost 10 m. With anchors at 13 m that leaves 65 cm of margin.
notes.p4c: Peak force lands around four times your body weight, which is the order real leash-fall measurements report (2–6 kN). That number matters as much as the depth: it is what your waist, the leash and the anchors take.
notes.p5: It is a quasi-static energy model, and deliberately conservative. It does not model damping, webbing hysteresis, leash-ring slippage, the energy your own body absorbs, or anchor compliance; and it assumes the webbing's rebound does not help stop you. All of that pushes real forces 10 to 30 % below what you see here. Use it to compare configurations and to spot that you do not have enough height — not as a design figure for an anchor.

field.leashRigid: The leash is treated as inextensible. A dynamic rope does stretch, but the webbing does 97 % of the braking, so ignoring it raises peak force by ~3 % and keeps the result on the safe side.
guide.title: Quick guide
guide.s1.title: SAG calculator
guide.s1.body: Works out how far your webbing sags with someone on it, and where you end up if you fall on the leash. Everything recalculates as you move the controls.
guide.s2.title: The chart is to scale
guide.s2.body: Same metre across as down. That is why a short slack line reads as a V and a long tight one as almost straight. It starts with the vertical axis exaggerated ×1.5 so the sag is easier to read: drop it to ×1 and the drawing is exact. You can drag the person along the webbing.
guide.s3.title: Scenarios and your own
guide.s3.body: The four scenarios load typical values for each discipline. Once your rig is dialled in, save it by name and come back to it with one tap. Same for your webbing.
guide.s4.title: The leash fall
guide.s4.body: The number that matters: how far your feet reach and how much ground is left. Also the peak force on your body and on the anchors. It is a conservative estimate — use it with margin.
guide.s5.title: Take it with you
guide.s5.body: Export to JPG, PNG or PDF, with or without the full data, with or without the chart. On a phone you can share it straight away.
field.noLeash: With no leash there is no fall to work out. Tricklines and longlines are walked untethered: you step off or jump, you do not end up hanging.
banner.tricklineJumps: Trickline: the jumping discipline. Rigged under very high tension — 8 to 11 kN at rest. During jumps, peaks on anchors and hardware easily reach {low}–{high} kN, with readings up to {extreme} kN on hard landings by heavier athletes. Those peaks are not in this calculation, which is static.
